issues.legal_issue: A claimant’s prior possession may support recovery of land from a later dispossessor when the claimant was forcibly dispossessed by that defendant rather than by the public owner.
material_facts: The plaintiff had been in possession of the disputed land before the Society took possession.
The Society claimed that the Government had evicted the plaintiff from the disputed land when it evicted him from adjoining land.

The evidence, including the eviction record and evidence about the land taken, supported the finding that the Government’s eviction concerned the adjoining land and that the Society later dispossessed the plaintiff from the disputed land.
The High Court’s finding of dispossession by the Society was upheld.
issues.conclusion: The Court accepted the finding that the Society dispossessed the plaintiff from the disputed land and found no basis to depart from the High Court’s conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: The determination turns on the evidence of what land was covered by the Government’s eviction and on the circumstances of the later taking of possession. The Court relied on the eviction record, witness testimony, the Society’s limited initial lease application, and the sequence of complaints and events.

rule.if: possession_recovery_proceeding and claimant_previously_possessed_land and defendant_claims_public_owner_evicted_claimant and evidence_shows_public_eviction_covered_only_other_land and evidence_shows_defendant_later_took_disputed_land

predicates.possession_recovery_proceeding: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking recovery of land from a person in possession.
predicates.claimant_previously_possessed_land: The claimant possessed the disputed land before the defendant took possession.
predicates.defendant_claims_public_owner_evicted_cl: The defendant asserted that the public owner had evicted the claimant from the disputed land.
predicates.evidence_shows_public_eviction_covered_o: The evidence showed that the public owner’s eviction concerned land other than the disputed land.
predicates.evidence_shows_defendant_later_took_disp: The evidence showed that the defendant later took possession of the disputed land.

issues.definition: When a claimant previously possessed land, the evidence shows the public owner evicted the claimant only from other land, and the defendant later took the disputed land, the defendant is found to have dispossessed the claimant.

issues.legal_issue: A suit for possession based on prior possession is maintainable after the summary possessory remedy’s short filing period has expired, unless the defendant establishes a better title or right to possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued for possession after being dispossessed from land he had previously possessed.
The suit was not brought under the summary remedy corresponding to section 9 of the Specific Relief Act; it was a regular suit for possession.
The Society argued that, after the summary remedy’s six-month period, a suit based on possession alone was incompetent.
Neither party established title to the disputed land, and the Society did not establish a right to possession derived from the State for the period before its later lease.
issues.conclusion: The suit was competent on the basis of prior possession, subject to the defendant’s ability to establish a better title or right to possession.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 8 and 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and the corresponding Travancore provisions, provide distinct remedies; section 8 prescribes use of the Code of Civil Procedure and does not bar a regular suit based on prior possession. Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars only suits whose cognizance is expressly or impliedly excluded. Articles 64 and 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, distinguish a possession-based suit from a title-based suit and were described as declaratory of the law. The Court relied on Mustapha Sahib v. Santha Pillai and Kuttan Narayaman v. Thomman Mathai, and considered Ram Harakh Rai v. Scheodihal Joti and the Allahabad Full Bench decision in Lachman v. Shambu Narain.

rule.if: regular_possession_suit and claimant_previously_possessed_land and claimant_dispossessed_by_defendant and suit_within_applicable_limitation and not defendant_establishes_better_right_to_possession

predicates.regular_possession_suit: The claimant brought a regular civil suit seeking possession rather than relying solely on a summary possessory remedy.
predicates.claimant_previously_possessed_land: The claimant possessed the disputed land before being dispossessed.
predicates.claimant_dispossessed_by_defendant: The defendant dispossessed the claimant from the disputed land.
predicates.suit_within_applicable_limitation: The claimant brought the suit within the limitation period applicable to the possession claim.
predicates.defendant_establishes_better_right_to_po: The defendant proved a title or other right to possession superior to the claimant’s prior possession.

issues.definition: A regular possession suit is maintainable on prior possession when the claimant was dispossessed by the defendant and the suit is timely, unless the defendant proves a better right to possession.

issues.legal_issue: Possession does not raise a presumption of title in favour of a party when the relevant facts are known and establish that neither party has title.
material_facts: The Society relied on its possession to invoke the presumption described in section 110 of the Evidence Act, 1872.
The facts concerning the parties’ possession and claims were known.
Neither party established title to the land at the relevant time.
issues.conclusion: The presumption under section 110 was immaterial; possession alone determined the dispute between the parties.
issues.legal_principle: Section 110 of the Evidence Act, 1872, may support a presumption of ownership from possession, but that presumption does not arise as a substitute for known facts that disclose no title in either party. In that situation, possession decides the contest between them.

predicates.possessory_dispute: The parties disputed the right to possess land.
predicates.relevant_facts_known: The material facts about possession and the parties’ claims were known.
predicates.neither_party_has_proven_title: Neither party established title to the disputed land.

issues.definition: When the facts are known and neither party proves title in a dispute about possession, possession decides the dispute between them.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant who has no better title or authority to possess land cannot defeat a prior possessor’s claim merely by asserting that an unconnected third party owns the land.
material_facts: The plaintiff had possessed the disputed land before the Society took possession.
The Society did not establish title in itself or authority from the State to take the land at the time of the dispossession.
The Society sought to resist the plaintiff’s claim by asserting that the State held title.
Neither party established title to the land at the relevant time.
issues.conclusion: The Society could not rely on the State’s asserted title as a defence to the plaintiff’s claim based on prior possession.
issues.legal_principle: A person in possession has a possessory title good against all persons except the rightful owner, and a defendant without a better title or authority cannot plead the jus tertii against that possession. The Court approved Perry v. Clissold, applied the principle in Asher v. Whitlock, Burling v. Read, and Smith v. Oxenden, and treated the conflicting approach in Doe v. Barnard as displaced. It distinguished Dharani Kanta Lahiri v. Garbar Ali Khan and Mahabir Prasad v. Jamuna Singh. The Court also referred to the declaratory effect of the amended Limitation Act.

rule.if: possession_recovery_proceeding and claimant_previously_possessed_land and defendant_wrongfully_dispossessed_claimant and defendant_lacks_better_title_or_owner_authority and defendant_relies_only_on_third_party_title

predicates.possession_recovery_proceeding: The claimant brought a proceeding to recover land from a person in possession.
predicates.claimant_previously_possessed_land: The claimant possessed the disputed land before the defendant took possession.
predicates.defendant_wrongfully_dispossessed_claima: The defendant took possession in a manner wrongful as against the claimant.
predicates.defendant_lacks_better_title_or_owner_au: The defendant established neither a superior title in itself nor authority from the rightful owner to take possession.
predicates.defendant_relies_only_on_third_party_tit: The defendant relied on an alleged title held by a third party unconnected to the defendant’s own right to possession.

issues.definition: A defendant who wrongfully dispossesses a prior possessor and has neither a better title nor the owner’s authority cannot defeat recovery by relying only on an unconnected third party’s title.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant’s prior possession is not barred from protection against a private defendant merely because occupation of the land was prohibited by regulations governing the relationship between the public authority and occupants.
material_facts: The Society argued that the plaintiff’s occupation of public land violated regulations that prohibited occupation and provided for fines and eviction.
The plaintiff sought recovery from the Society, a private defendant, and did not need to rely on the illegality of his occupation to establish prior possession and dispossession.
The regulations governed the relationship between the Government and persons occupying its land; the stated penalty for wrongful occupation was a fine, not punishment for a crime.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff’s claim could not be refused on the ground that his original possession was unlawful under the regulations.
issues.legal_principle: The regulations concerning occupation of public land regulated the relationship between Government and occupants and did not determine competing claims to possession between private persons. The principle in Holman v. Johnson that a court may refuse assistance where a claimant must rely on illegality did not apply because the plaintiff did not need to rely on his unlawful occupation to recover possession.

predicates.possession_recovery_proceeding: The claimant brought a proceeding to recover land from a person in possession.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_prior_possession_not_: The claimant relied on prior possession and dispossession rather than on the unlawful act as a necessary element of the claim.
predicates.defendant_is_private_person: The person resisting the claim was a private party rather than the public authority that administered the occupation rule.
predicates.occupation_rule_governs_public_authority: The rule restricting occupation governed the relationship between the public authority and persons occupying its land.

issues.definition: A private defendant cannot use a public-land occupation restriction to defeat a claim based on prior possession when that restriction governs the public authority’s relationship with occupants and the claimant need not rely on illegality.

issues.legal_issue: A court may allow a late amendment relying on a subsequent event when the amendment enables the dispute to be resolved in the existing proceeding and avoids further litigation without unfairly taking the opposing party by surprise.
material_facts: During the suit, the Society received a further lease over part of the disputed land.
The Society’s written statement did not plead that lease as a basis for its defence, and it sought amendment only at the end of the High Court appeal, after a lengthy delay.
The documents concerning the lease were already on the record, the proposed amendment remained within the subject matter of the suit, and the opposing party could answer the new plea.
Without the amendment, a separate suit concerning the later lease would be inevitable; allowing the amendment would permit the issue to be tried on remand and reduce litigation.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the amendment concerning the later lease and remanded the dispute over the affected portion for trial of the issue raised by the amendment.
issues.legal_principle: Amendment is discretionary, and delay does not invariably preclude it where the amendment allows complete justice, does not open an unrelated case or unfairly surprise the other party, and avoids circuity of action. Subsequent events may be considered when they reduce litigation. The Court relied on Ram Ratan Sahu v. Mohant Sahu, Raicharan Mandal v. Biswanath Mandal, Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chandhuri, Patterson v. State of Alabama, Surinder Kumar v. Gian Chand, and the amendment authorities L. J. Leach & Co. v. Jardine Skinner & Co., Pungonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil, and A. K. Gupta & Sons v. Damodar Valley Corporation; it distinguished the authorities relied on against amendment, including Ma Shwe Mya v. Maung Mo Huaung and Kanda v. Waghu.

rule.if: civil_appeal and proposed_amendment_relies_on_subsequent_event and amendment_within_existing_dispute and opposing_party_can_answer_new_plea and amendment_avoids_separate_litigation and amendment_will_not_unfairly_surprise_opponent

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is a civil appeal in which the court can consider a proposed pleading amendment.
predicates.proposed_amendment_relies_on_subsequent_: The proposed amendment relies on an event that occurred after the original pleading.
predicates.amendment_within_existing_dispute: The amendment concerns the same underlying dispute rather than introducing an unrelated case.
predicates.opposing_party_can_answer_new_plea: The opposing party has an opportunity to contest the new plea.
predicates.amendment_avoids_separate_litigation: Allowing the amendment enables the issue to be determined in the existing proceeding instead of requiring a separate suit.
predicates.amendment_will_not_unfairly_surprise_opp: The amendment does not unfairly take the opposing party by surprise.

issues.definition: A late amendment based on a later event is allowed and the issue remanded when it remains within the existing dispute, can be answered, avoids separate litigation, and causes no unfair surprise.

issues.legal_issue: A later grant of a right to possess land operates prospectively when its formal document is unambiguous and does not make the grant retrospective.
material_facts: The Society received a second lease during the pending suit over part of the disputed land.
The formal lease document did not state that the grant was retrospective.

Other documents recorded a demand for rent calculated from the date of the earlier lease, but the Court considered that this could follow from rules requiring rent from a person in unlawful possession or reflect the official’s interpretation.
issues.conclusion: If the second lease is valid, it must be read as operating from the date of its grant and cannot be treated as retrospective to the first lease.
issues.legal_principle: A formal, unambiguous instrument cannot be varied by reference to other documents not intended to vary it. The effect of the later lease was left for determination at trial, but the Court held that it could not operate retrospectively absent such a term in the instrument.

predicates.later_land_grant_disputed: The parties dispute the effect of a grant of a right to possess land made after the original dispute began.
predicates.formal_grant_document_unambiguous: The formal document granting the right is unambiguous.
predicates.formal_grant_document_contains_no_retroa: The formal grant document does not state that the grant applies retrospectively.

issues.definition: A later land grant operates prospectively when the formal grant document is unambiguous and contains no term making it retrospective.

issues.legal_issue: A possession decree remains enforceable for the portion of land unaffected by a later grant, while the portion affected by that grant requires a further determination after amendment.
material_facts: The suit covered two portions of disputed land.
The Society’s later lease concerned only one portion, and the Court allowed amendment of the written statement to plead that lease.
The later lease did not affect the Court’s determination concerning the other portion.
The appeal was dismissed as to the unaffected portion and the dispute concerning the leased portion was remanded for trial of the amended issue.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed as to the portion unaffected by the later lease; as to the portion covered by that lease, the amendment was allowed and the matter was remanded for determination of the lease’s effect and related relief.
issues.legal_principle: A subsequent event affecting only part of the disputed property may be considered through an allowed amendment without disturbing the decision concerning the unaffected part. The Court also held that the later lease could not be treated as retrospective and left its remaining legal effect, along with related mesne profits and improvements, for determination on remand.

predicates.appeal_from_possession_decree: The matter is an appeal from a decree awarding possession of disputed land.
predicates.later_grant_affects_only_part_of_dispute: A later grant concerns only part of the land covered by the decree.
predicates.amendment_allowed_for_affected_part: The pleadings are amended to raise the effect of the later grant on the affected part.

issues.definition: When a later grant affects only part of land covered by a possession decree and an amendment is allowed, the decree stands for the unaffected part and the affected part is remanded.
